questions.explanation: The "down and out" eye position is the classic sign of an oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. CN III supplies the superior, inferior, and medial recti, as well as the inferior oblique. When these are paralyzed, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) act unopposed, pulling the eye outward and downward. The accompanying ptosis results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris, also supplied by CN III. 4th nerve palsy (Option A) causes vertical diplopia and an "up and in" eye position. 6th nerve palsy (Option C) results in an "inward" deviation (esotropia) due to medial rectus action. 7th nerve palsy (Option D) affects facial expression and eye closure but not eye position. Thus, the "down and out" triad with ptosis confirms CN III involvement

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A posterior staphyloma was observed on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia (outpouching) of the posterior sclera. It is most commonly seen in pathological or high myopia. Progressive elongation of the globe in myopia leads to mechanical stretching and thinning of the posterior pole, resulting in this structural deformity. Hypermetropia (Option B) involves a shorter axial length and is not associated with scleral ectasia. Primary open-angle glaucoma (Option C) causes optic nerve cupping but not global scleral thinning. Retinitis pigmentosa (Option D) is characterized by "bone-spicule" pigmentation and vessel attenuation, not staphylomas. Therefore, posterior staphyloma is a hallmark diagnostic feature of degenerative high axial myopia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. On evaluation, a diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome is made. Which cranial nerves are compressed in this condition?
questions.explanation: Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of the structures passing through the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone. These include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Compression leads to total ophthalmoplegia (inability to move the eye) and ptosis. The maxillary nerve (V2) (Option B) is not affected because it passes through the foramen rotundum. The optic nerve (CN II) (Options C and D) is also spared because it enters the orbit through the separate optic canal. Thus, any syndrome resulting in extraocular muscle paralysis along with sensory loss in the forehead (V1) but sparing vision (CN II) and the mid-face (V2) specifically localizes to the superior orbital fissure

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A doctor receives two court summons—one to appear as a witness in a murder case and another to give expert medical testimony. Which summons should the doctor attend as a priority?
options: Appearance for providing medical expert opinion
questions.explanation: A criminal court summons in a murder case carries a legal imperative and higher priority over other civil or expert witness duties. Legal attendance is mandatory unless a legitimate legal excuse is provided. While providing an expert medical opinion is professionally significant, a direct court order in a criminal matter represents a primary legal obligation that the doctor must prioritize. Appearance for expert opinion (Option B) is considered important but is typically subordinate to a direct criminal court summons. The timing of receipt (Option C) is irrelevant, as the chronological order of summonses does not override the legal gravity and mandatory nature of a criminal case involving a serious offense like murder. Therefore, the doctor must attend the criminal court first to fulfill their judicial duty in the murder trial, ensuring compliance with the law's highest mandates

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman is found dead in a locked room, and during autopsy it is noted that a heat stove was still running inside the room. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.explanation: A running stove in a confined, locked space is the classic environment for carbon monoxide (CO) accumulation due to incomplete combustion. CO has an affinity for hemoglobin roughly 250 times that of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and preventing oxygen transport, which leads to fatal tissue hypoxia. Autopsy typically reveals a characteristic cherry-red post-mortem staining. Cyanide poisoning (Option B) usually results from industrial accidents and shows brick-red staining. H2S poisoning (Option C) occurs in industrial settings or sewers and is identified by a rotten-egg odor and bluish-green staining. Aluminium phosphide (Option D) is common in agricultural suicide cases and releases phosphine gas, which causes cardiac toxicity rather than enclosed-room asphyxiation. Based on the household heating scenario and the high risk of CO buildup, carbon monoxide poisoning is the most probable cause of death

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person is found dead in a swimming pool. Autopsy reveals water in the stomach and lungs, along with fine mucoid froth at the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death?
questions.explanation: Wet drowning is the mode of death in approximately 90% of drowning cases and occurs when water is actively inhaled into the respiratory tract. This aspiration leads to the washout of pulmonary surfactant, alveolar collapse, and terminal asphyxia. The pathognomonic autopsy findings for wet drowning include copious, persistent mucoid froth at the nostrils and mouth, as well as overdistended, water-logged lungs and water in the stomach from swallowing. Dry drowning (Option A) occurs due to severe reflex laryngospasm that prevents water from entering the lungs; in these cases, the lungs remain dry. Near drowning (Option C) refers to a scenario where the individual survives for at least 24 hours after the event. Cardiac arrest (Option D) is a non-specific terminal event. Thus, the presence of lung water and froth confirms wet drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old apparently healthy man, who was found to be carrying laxatives and an enema apparatus, develops abdominal pain at the airport. An abdominal X-ray is performed and shows the given findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Body packer syndrome, or "surgical mules syndrome," involves the intentional swallowing or internal planting of drug-filled packets (usually wrapped in condoms or plastic) for smuggling. The patient's history of carrying laxatives and enemas is a major clue, as smugglers use these to facilitate the expulsion of the packets. The abdominal X-ray demonstrates characteristic cylindrical, radio-opaque objects within the GI tract. Bezoar syndrome (Option A) involves an indigestible mass, such as hair, but would not appear as multiple discrete cylindrical containers. Pica (Option B) involves eating non-food items like soil but doesn't present with this specific packaging or medical kit. Fecalith (Option D) is a hard mass of stool that can cause obstruction but typically shows generalized bloating on X-ray rather than distinct containers. Thus, the X-ray findings and airport context confirm body packing

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with lung injury and rupture of the tympanic membrane following exposure to a blast. These findings are characteristic of which category of blast wave effect?
questions.explanation: Blast injuries are categorized by the physical mechanism of trauma. Primary (Level I) blast injuries result directly from the overpressure shock wave impacting the body. This wave most severely affects air-filled organs due to their unique density compared to surrounding tissues. Therefore, tympanic membrane rupture and blast lung injury (alveolar-capillary disruption) are pathognomonic Level I injuries. Level II injuries are caused by flying debris hitting the body. Level III injuries occur when the individual is physically thrown by the wind of the blast. Level IV injuries encompass all other effects, such as burns, toxic gas inhalation, or building collapse. Because the pressure wave itself is responsible for rupturing the eardrum and damaging the lung parenchyma, these findings specifically categorize the effect as a primary or Level I blast injury

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During an explosion, a patient sustains a crushed injury to the lower limb due to collapse of a building. Which type of blast injury does this represent?
questions.explanation: Blast injuries are classified by their physical mechanism. Quaternary injuries are miscellaneous trauma resulting from the blast, including crush injuries from building collapses, burns, and traumatic asphyxia. Primary blast injuries (Option A) result directly from the air compression wave (overpressure) and typically damage hollow organs like the ears (tympanic membrane), lungs, and GIT. Secondary blast injuries (Option B) are caused by flying missiles or projectiles propelled by the blast hitting the body. Tertiary blast injuries (Option C) occur when the individual is physically lifted and thrown against the ground or walls, often leading to fractures or dislocations. A quinary injury category (Option E) also exists for injuries from environmental contaminants like radiation or chemicals. Since this specific patient suffered a crush injury from a structural collapse, it is definitively classified as a quaternary injury

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness, and episodes of syncope. On examination, the pulse is irregularly irregular. What finding is most likely to be observed on jugular venous pressure (JVP) examination?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of atrial fibrillation (AF), often referred to as "Holiday Heart Syndrome" in this context. The jugular venous pulse (JVP) reflects pressure changes in the right atrium; specifically, the 'a' wave is produced by active atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively in a coordinated manner; instead, they undergo rapid, disorganized electrical activity. Consequently, there is a complete loss of the organized atrial systole required to produce the 'a' wave, leading to its disappearance on the JVP tracing. Large 'a' waves (Option B) occur during resistance to atrial emptying, such as in tricuspid stenosis. Cannon 'a' waves (Option C) are seen when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block. A steep 'y' descent (Option D) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis. Thus, the absent 'a' wave is the definitive JVP finding for AF

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever is found on examination to have a loud first heart sound and a mid-diastolic murmur. Which valvular heart disease is most likely present?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of rheumatic fever combined with the auscultatory findings of a loud S1 and a mid-diastolic murmur are classic indicators of Mitral Stenosis (MS). Rheumatic heart disease is the leading cause of MS worldwide, resulting in the thickening and fusion of valve leaflets. The S1 is loud because the stiffened valves close forcefully at the start of systole. The mid-diastolic murmur occurs due to turbulent blood flow across the narrowed mitral orifice as the left ventricle fills. While Tricuspid Stenosis (TS) (Option A) also produces a mid-diastolic murmur, it typically increases with inspiration and is rarely seen in isolation. Mitral Regurgitation (MR) (Option B) presents with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Aortic Regurgitation (AR) (Option D) produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Therefore, based on the specific location and nature of the murmur following rheumatic fever, Mitral Stenosis is the most accurate diagnosis for this patient

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following genetic mutations is most commonly associated with familial cases of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder that destroys motor neurons. Approximately 10% of cases are familial, and the most common genetic cause identified in these instances is a mutation in the SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) gene. This mutation leads to a toxic gain-of-function in the SOD1 protein, triggering motor neuron death through oxidative stress and protein aggregation. The CFTR mutation (Option A) is the cause of cystic fibrosis, affecting chloride transport in epithelial cells. The HTT mutation (Option C) involves a CAG repeat expansion causing Huntington's disease. The FMR1 mutation (Option D) results in Fragile X syndrome, the leading inherited cause of intellectual disability. Therefore, SOD1 remains the definitive genetic marker for familial ALS

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency room with central chest pain and has a known history of heart disease. An ECG is provided. Based on the ECG findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided ECG demonstrates significant ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads (V2-V4) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). Crucially, there is reciprocal ST-segment depression in the inferior leads (III and aVF), which is a hallmark finding that differentiates a myocardial infarction (MI) from other conditions like pericarditis. This pattern indicates an acute injury involving the anterior wall (supplied by the LAD) and the lateral wall (supplied by the LCX or diagonal branches). Inferolateral MI (Option B) is incorrect because it would require ST elevation in inferior leads, whereas they show depression here. Acute pericarditis (Option C) typically presents with diffuse ST elevation across most leads and lacks localized reciprocal changes. Constrictive pericarditis (Option D) is a chronic condition characterized by low voltage QRS or nonspecific changes rather than acute ST elevation. Thus, the localized elevations and reciprocal depressions confirm an Anterolateral MI

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia following a myocardial infarction. His blood pressure is 120/85 mm Hg, and the ECG findings are provided. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a broad QRS complex (>120 ms), regular, monomorphic tachycardia following an MI, which is diagnostic of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). With a blood pressure of 120/85 mm Hg, the patient is hemodynamically stable. According to ACLS guidelines, the first-line pharmacological treatment for stable VT is IV amiodarone. Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that suppresses ventricular ectopy and is safe in structural heart disease. Labetalol (Option B) is an antihypertensive and has no role in acute VT termination. Metoprolol (Option C), while used post-MI for prevention, is not the primary choice for terminating an active VT episode and carries a risk of hypotension. Nitroglycerin (Option D) is used for ischemic chest pain but does not treat the underlying arrhythmia. Therefore, IV amiodarone is the most appropriate intervention for this stable, post-MI tachycardia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with weight gain, hair thinning, and dry skin and is diagnosed with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Which autoantibody is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a chronic autoimmune condition and the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. It is characterized by the presence of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, which target the TPO enzyme essential for thyroid hormone synthesis. These antibodies mediate the autoimmune destruction of the gland, leading to the patient's symptoms of weight gain, hair thinning, and dry skin. Anti-TSH antibodies (Option B) are not a diagnostic marker for this condition. Anti-TBG antibodies (Option C) are rare and lack clinical relevance for Hashimoto’s diagnosis. Long-acting thyroid-stimulating antibodies (LATS) (Option D) are pathognomonic for Graves' disease, which causes hyperthyroidism rather than the hypothyroidism seen in Hashimoto's. Laboratory confirmation of Hashimoto's typically relies on elevated TSH, low free T4, and positive anti-TPO titers. Therefore, anti-TPO is the most relevant diagnostic antibody

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An RTA patient has received 4 packed RBC within a few hours. Which of the following will be seen?
questions.explanation: Stored packed red blood cells (PRBCs) contain citrate as an anticoagulant. During rapid or massive blood transfusions, the large volume of citrate enters the recipient's bloodstream and binds to ionized calcium. This chelation leads to acute hypocalcemia. While the liver normally metabolizes citrate, this process is often impaired in trauma patients due to shock or hypothermia. Clinical manifestations include paresthesia, muscle cramps, and a prolonged QT interval. Hypernatremia (Option A) and hyponatremia (Option B) are not typical complications of PRBC transfusion as the sodium content in the preservative is minimal. While hyperkalemia (Option D) can occur due to potassium leakage from older stored cells, hypocalcemia resulting from citrate toxicity is a more classic and specifically tested metabolic complication of rapid PRBC administration. Therefore, monitoring ionized calcium levels is essential during emergency resuscitation involving multiple units of blood

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive limb weakness over the past year. Examination reveals muscle fasciculations and increased muscle tone, with preserved sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the simultaneous involvement of both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN). The presence of hypertonia (a UMN sign) and muscle fasciculations (an LMN sign) in the same limb, while the sensory system remains intact, is pathognomonic for ALS. Spinal Muscular Atrophy (Option B) is a pure LMN disease and would not present with UMN signs like hypertonia. Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (Option C) typically presents with pure LMN weakness that is often asymmetric and lacks UMN features. Becker Muscular Dystrophy (Option D) is a genetic myopathy that causes proximal muscle weakness but does not involve motor neurons, meaning it lacks fasciculations and UMN signs. Because ALS relentlessly destroys both sets of motor neurons in the motor cortex and spinal cord while sparing sensory pathways, it is the only viable diagnosis for this clinical picture

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with symmetrical weakness of the lower limbs accompanied by areflexia. He gives a history of diarrhoea two weeks prior and is diagnosed with Guillain–Barré syndrome. What is the underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy often triggered by a preceding gastrointestinal infection, such as Campylobacter jejuni. The pathophysiology involves autoantibodies attacking the myelin sheath of peripheral nerves. GBS primarily affects large-diameter myelinated fibers, including A-fibers (motor and sensory) and B-fibers (preganglionic autonomic). This widespread demyelination disrupts motor signals and reflex arcs, leading to the classic presentation of symmetrical ascending weakness and areflexia. Option B is incorrect because B-fibers are not affected in isolation. Options C and D are incorrect because GBS is a disease of the peripheral nervous system and nerve roots, not the central spinal cord. Cord inflammation would typically present with upper motor neuron signs and a sensory level, which are absent in GBS. Thus, the demyelination of both A and B peripheral nerve fibers is the correct underlying cause

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic cough and weight loss for three months. Biopsy of a lung mass shows tumor cells expressing chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely to be associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of chromogranin and synaptophysin on lung biopsy indicates a neuroendocrine tumor, most likely small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). SCLC is highly notorious for producing ectopic hormones. The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with SCLC is the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH), caused by ectopic ADH production. Hypercalcemia (Option A) is more classically associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung due to PTHrP secretion. While SCLC can cause Cushing syndrome via ectopic ACTH, SIADH is more frequently encountered in clinical practice for this tumor type. Gynaecomastia (Option C) is associated with certain germ cell tumors or liver disease, not neuroendocrine lung cancers. Therefore, given the specific neuroendocrine markers identified in the biopsy, SIADH is the most likely paraneoplastic manifestation to observe in this patient

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with episodic palpitations, headache, and excessive sweating, with a blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating in a hypertensive patient is highly suggestive of a pheochromocytoma. This is a catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. The measurement of 24-hour urinary metanephrines (metabolites of epinephrine and norepinephrine) is the most sensitive diagnostic test to confirm catecholamine excess. Carcinoid tumors (Option A) and carcinoid crisis (Option C) present with flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm, and are diagnosed by urinary 5-HIAA rather than metanephrines. Neuroblastoma (Option D) is a pediatric tumor that can arise in the adrenal medulla but is typically diagnosed in children by elevated dopamine metabolites (HVA/VMA) and presents differently than the adult paroxysmal symptoms seen here. Given the specific clinical symptoms and the elevation of metanephrines, pheochromocytoma is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain consistent with a cluster headache. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: High-flow 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min) administered via a non-rebreather mask is the gold standard for the acute abortive treatment of a cluster headache attack. It typically provides rapid relief within 15–20 minutes and is highly effective with a superior safety profile. Verapamil (Option A) is the first-line choice for long-term prophylaxis to prevent future attacks but is ineffective for stopping an acute episode once it has started. Lithium (Option C) and Topiramate (Option D) are also used as prophylactic agents in chronic or refractory cases rather than for acute relief. Cluster headaches are characterized by severe, unilateral, retro-orbital pain accompanied by autonomic symptoms like lacrimation or nasal congestion. Because the attacks are short-lived but excruciating, rapid-acting treatments like oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan are prioritized. Therefore, high-flow oxygen is the most appropriate immediate intervention

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT imaging reveals a renal mass, and the aldosterone–renin ratio (ARR) is elevated. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The combination of hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, a high Aldosterone-Renin Ratio (ARR), and a localized adrenal mass is highly suggestive of an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn’s Syndrome). In cases of confirmed unilateral adrenal disease in a surgical candidate, laparoscopic adrenalectomy is the definitive treatment of choice as it can cure the underlying hyperaldosteronism. Medical management with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like Spironolactone (Option A) is generally reserved for patients with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or those who are not fit for surgery. The ACTH stimulation test (Option C) is used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease), which presents with hypotension and hyperkalemia. The Dexamethasone suppression test (Option D) is the standard investigation for Cushing’s syndrome, which involves cortisol excess. Given the evidence of a unilateral functional tumor, surgical removal is the most appropriate management step

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man has had persistent hypercalcemia for the past 1.5 years, with parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels within the normal range. What is the most likely underlying cause of his hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: Chronic hypercalcemia with a normal or low Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) level indicates a PTH-independent cause of calcium elevation. In Sarcoidosis, activated macrophages within non-caseating granulomas express the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase. This enzyme converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption and persistent hypercalcemia. Malignancy (Option A) often causes acute, symptomatic hypercalcemia through bone metastasis or PTHrP secretion, but the chronic, stable 1.5-year history is more typical of a granulomatous disease. Parathyroid hyperplasia (Option C) would result in primary hyperparathyroidism, characterized by an inappropriately elevated PTH level. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (Option D) typically presents with hypocalcemia in the early stages and secondary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH) later on. Thus, the extra-renal production of calcitriol in Sarcoidosis best explains this metabolic profile

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On examination, a person has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and a shift of the trachea. What is the management?
options: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion
questions.explanation: The clinical signs of respiratory distress, distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return), absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and contralateral tracheal deviation are diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax. This is a surgical emergency where air under pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, potentially leading to obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression using a wide-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space (midclavicular line) or the 4th/5th intercostal space (anterior axillary line) is life-saving and must be performed before obtaining imaging. Waiting for a chest X-ray (Option A) is dangerous as it delays critical treatment. Pericardiocentesis (Option C) is the treatment for cardiac tamponade. Pleurodesis (Option D) is used to prevent recurrence in stable patients but has no role in acute emergency stabilization. Definitive chest tube thoracostomy should follow the initial needle decompression

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea, and laboratory testing shows elevated serum prolactin levels. MRI of the brain reveals a pituitary adenoma. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with hyperprolactinemia due to a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH, leading to the clinical triad of amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility. The first-line medical treatment for prolactinomas is dopamine agonists, such as Bromocriptine or Cabergoline. These medications effectively inhibit prolactin secretion and can lead to significant tumor shrinkage. Bromocriptine is particularly favored in women desiring pregnancy due to its established safety profile. Letrozole (Option B) is an aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer and ovulation induction. Tamoxifen (Option C) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used in breast cancer management. Goserelin (Option D) is a GnRH agonist used for endometriosis and prostate cancer. Surgical resection is only considered if medical therapy fails or if there are severe compressive symptoms like vision loss. Therefore, dopamine agonist therapy remains the primary intervention

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness, back pain, and recurrent infections. Evaluation reveals an M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis. Which factor is most important in determining the prognosis in this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of bone pain, recurrent infections, and an "M spike" on electrophoresis is diagnostic of Multiple Myeloma. The International Staging System (ISS), which is the standard model for determining prognosis in these patients, relies on two specific laboratory values: serum albumin and serum beta-2 microglobulin. Beta-2 microglobulin serves as a marker for tumor burden and renal function; higher levels indicate a poorer prognosis. Albumin reflects the patient's general nutritional and inflammatory status; lower levels are associated with more aggressive disease. IgG (Option A) is the most common paraprotein but is not a component of the ISS. IgM (Option B) is associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia. While LDH (Option C) can be used in the Revised-ISS, the classic ISS relies primarily on the combination of albumin and beta-2 microglobulin for its three prognostic stages

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man has the following hepatitis B serological profile: HBsAg positive, IgM anti- HBc negative, IgG anti-HBc positive, and HBeAg positive. Based on this serological status, what is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: The serological profile indicates chronic active Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBsAg positivity indicates ongoing infection, while negative IgM anti-HBc and positive IgG anti-HBc confirm that the disease is in the chronic phase rather than acute. The presence of HBeAg signifies high viral replication and increased infectivity. Antiviral therapy is required to suppress viral replication and prevent liver damage. Lamivudine is an oral nucleoside analog that inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and is an effective (though older) treatment option for chronic HBV. Ombitasvir (Option B) is used for Hepatitis C (HCV), not HBV. Ritonavir (Option C) and Abacavir (Option D) are components of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV and are not standard treatments for HBV monoinfection. While tenofovir and entecavir are now preferred first-line due to lower resistance rates, Lamivudine is the only appropriate HBV drug listed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with renal tubular acidosis (RTA) presents with red-colored urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following findings is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of myoglobinuria following trauma indicates rhabdomyolysis, where massive muscle breakdown releases cell contents into the bloodstream. This includes myoglobin, which is highly nephrotoxic and often leads to acute tubular necrosis (ATN), and large amounts of intracellular potassium. Consequently, hyperkalemia is a hallmark feature of this condition due to both the direct release from damaged myocytes and impaired renal excretion from the subsequent kidney injury. Hypernatremia (Option A) and hyponatremia (Option C) are not typical hallmark findings in this clinical scenario. Hypokalemia (Option D) is seen in distal (Type 1) and proximal (Type 2) renal tubular acidosis (RTA), but rhabdomyolysis-induced kidney injury typically presents with hyperkalemia (often mirroring Type 4 RTA physiology). Therefore, monitoring and treating elevated potassium levels is a critical priority in patients with suspected rhabdomyolysis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient after RTA had a renal shut down. Work-up shows: FeNa: < 1%, Urine osmolality: 300 mOsm/kg, Urinary sodium: 40 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s laboratory findings point toward intrinsic renal damage, specifically Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN). In ATN, damaged tubules lose the ability to concentrate urine and reabsorb sodium. The urinary sodium of 40 mEq/L is elevated, indicating sodium wasting, and the urine osmolality of ~300 mOsm/kg reflects "isosthenuria," where the kidney can no longer produce concentrated or dilute urine compared to plasma. Although a Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FeNa) < 1% is typically associated with pre-renal states, it can also be seen in early or non-oliguric ATN. Pre-renal AKI (Option B) is characterized by a lower urinary sodium (< 20 mEq/L) and a much higher urine osmolality (> 500 mOsm/kg). Post-renal AKI (Option C) requires evidence of obstruction on imaging. "Renal AKI" (Option D) is a broad category; ATN is the specific pathological diagnosis that matches the electrolyte wasting and osmolality findings

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What defect is seen in Bernard Soulier syndrome?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder characterized by a primary defect in platelet adhesion. The underlying pathology is a deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) complex. This complex acts as the essential receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF); without it, platelets cannot adhere to the exposed subendothelial matrix during vascular injury. Patients typically present with mucocutaneous bleeding and thrombocytopenia with characteristic "giant platelets" on a peripheral smear. Deficiency of the GpIIb/IIIa receptor (Option A) is seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which affects platelet aggregation. Deficiency of von Willebrand factor (Option C) defines von Willebrand disease. Deficiency of ADP receptors (Option D) occurs in rare disorders like P2Y12 defects, impacting the aggregation pathway. Therefore, the GpIb receptor defect is the specific hallmark of Bernard-Soulier syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath over the past six months, along with a dry cough. On auscultation, bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations are heard. There is no history of fever, joint pain, or occupational exposure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing lung disease typically seen in older adults. The clinical presentation of worsening exertional dyspnea and a nonproductive cough over several months is classic. The most characteristic physical finding on auscultation is bilateral basal end-inspiratory "Velcro" crackles (crepitations). The diagnosis of "idiopathic" is supported by the absence of systemic symptoms like fever, joint pain, or any known occupational exposures. Cor-pulmonale (Option A) refers to right heart failure resulting from chronic lung disease, not the primary lung disease itself. Sarcoidosis (Option B) usually presents with systemic features and hilar lymphadenopathy. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Option D) is typically linked to a clear history of organic dust exposure (e.g., birds or mold) and often has a more acute or subacute onset. Therefore, the described presentation is most consistent with IPF

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with weakness of the face, arm, and leg on the side opposite to the lesion. Non-contrast CT of the brain shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. What is the most likely anatomical location of the bleed?
questions.explanation: Intracerebral hemorrhages (ICH) that result in dense contralateral hemiparesis (weakness of the face, arm, and leg) most commonly occur in the basal ganglia, particularly the putamen. Bleeding in this region compresses the adjacent internal capsule, through which the corticospinal fibers pass, leading to widespread motor deficits on the opposite side of the body. Midbrain lesions (Option B) often cause oculomotor nerve palsies in addition to motor weakness but are less common sites for primary ICH. Pontine hemorrhages (Option C) frequently result in quadriplegia or "locked-in" syndrome rather than simple hemiparesis. Medullary hemorrhages (Option D) are rare and typically present with contralateral limb weakness combined with ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits (Wallenberg syndrome). Given the classic presentation of hemi-weakness, the basal ganglia is the most statistically and clinically likely location

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman reports episodes of chest pain occurring predominantly on waking up in the early morning, with symptoms being more frequent during the winter months. Which clinical condition best explains this presentation?
options: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms are highly characteristic of Prinzmetal's (variant) angina. This condition is caused by transient coronary artery vasospasms that typically occur at rest, often in the early morning hours, and are frequently triggered by cold weather. These spasms can be induced by various vasoconstrictors, including acetylcholine (Ach). Fixed plaque obstruction (Option A) and increased demand (Option C) describe the pathophysiology of stable exertional angina, where pain occurs during physical activity, not at rest. While sympathomimetic drive (Option D) increases in the morning, it does not specifically explain the rest-related vasospasm seen in variant angina as well as the Ach-induced mechanism does. Prinzmetal's angina is unique because the ECG may show transient ST-segment elevation during the attack, which resolves completely once the spasm subsides

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: CSF shows abundant PMNs with low sugar and elevated proteins. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Acute bacterial meningitis (ABM) is characterized by a specific set of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings: a predominance of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), low glucose levels (due to consumption by bacteria and impaired transport), and significantly elevated protein levels (resulting from blood-brain barrier damage). Tubercular meningitis (Option B) typically presents with a lymphocytic predominance and very high protein levels, although PMNs may be seen early in the disease. Viral meningitis and encephalitis (Options C and D) generally show a lymphocytic predominance with normal or only slightly reduced glucose levels and mild protein elevation. The gross appearance of the CSF in ABM is often turbid or purulent, reflecting the high neutrophil count. Therefore, the provided laboratory values are the classic diagnostic signature for an acute bacterial etiology

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: After an initial serum β-hCG test in a patient with suspected pregnancy, when should the repeat β-hCG level ideally be checked to assess viability or progression?
questions.explanation: In early pregnancy, the doubling time of serum β-hCG is a critical marker of trophoblastic health and pregnancy viability. The standard clinical practice is to repeat the test after 48 hours. In a viable intrauterine pregnancy, the β-hCG level is expected to rise by at least 66% over this 48-hour window. A slower rise or a plateau in levels is highly suspicious of an ectopic pregnancy, while falling levels typically indicate an ongoing miscarriage. Checking after 24 hours (Option A) is often too early to see a meaningful trend, while 72 or 96 hours (Options C and D) may delay a critical diagnosis if the patient is unstable. Additionally, the "discriminatory zone" (usually ≥1,500 IU/L) is used alongside these trends to confirm the presence of a gestational sac on ultrasound

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents for emergency contraception within a few hours of unprotected sexual intercourse and prefers a single-dose option rather than multiple pills. What would be the most appropriate recommendation in this case?
questions.explanation: For emergency contraception (EC) following unprotected intercourse, Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is the most appropriate single-pill regimen. This progestin-only pill is highly effective when taken within 72 hours and fulfills the patient's preference for a single dose. It also avoids the high risk of nausea and vomiting associated with estrogen-containing pills. Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg (Option A) requires two doses taken 12 hours apart, which is less convenient. The combination regimen (Option B), known as the Yuzpe regimen, is less effective and has more side effects. Desogestrel 3 mg (Option D) is a daily contraceptive and is not a standard drug for emergency use. While the copper IUD is the most effective EC method, among oral options, the 1.5 mg single-dose levonorgestrel is the clinical standard

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The waveform shown in the image represents which of the following physiological parameters?
questions.explanation: The provided image is a capnogram, which measures the concentration of carbon dioxide in the exhaled air. Specifically, it represents End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2). The waveform shows the transition from inspiration (zero CO2) to the rapid rise of mixed air during expiration, concluding with the alveolar plateau. The highest point at the end of expiration (Point E) is the EtCO2 value. Arterial oxygen saturation (Option A) is measured by pulse oximetry and displayed as a plethysmographic waveform. Functional residual capacity (Option C) is a volume measurement that cannot be visualized on a real-time monitor. Tidal volume (Option D) is the amount of air inhaled/exhaled, which can be inferred from respiration but is not the parameter directly plotted on this CO2 concentration graph. Capnography is essential for confirming ET tube placement and monitoring ventilation quality

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is brought after a road traffic accident and imaging reveals the fracture shown. What type of fracture is this?
questions.explanation: The X-ray depicts a fracture occurring in the region between the greater and lesser trochanters of the proximal femur. This is an intertrochanteric fracture, which is extra-capsular in nature. Because it is outside the hip joint capsule, the blood supply to the femoral head remains relatively well-preserved, leading to a much lower risk of avascular necrosis compared to neck fractures. Subtrochanteric fractures (Option A) occur below the lesser trochanter in the femoral shaft. Femoral neck fractures (Option C) occur superior to the trochanters and within the joint capsule (intracapsular). Pubic rami fractures (Option D) involve the pelvic ring and not the femur itself. Intertrochanteric fractures are often comminuted and result from high-energy trauma in young patients or simple falls in the elderly. Based on the specific bony landmarks, the diagnosis is confirmed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly woman involved in a road traffic accident presents with respiratory distress and altered sensorium. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated D-dimer levels, and the chest X-ray demonstrates suggestive findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of respiratory distress and altered mental status following a high-energy accident (likely involving long bone fractures) is diagnostic of Fat Embolism Syndrome. This occurs when fat globules from bone marrow are released into the bloodstream and travel to the lungs and brain. Respiratory distress usually manifests 24–72 hours after trauma due to capillary obstruction. Gas gangrene (Option A) presents with crepitus and foul discharge. Acute infection (Option C) typically presents with fever rather than sudden post-traumatic hypoxia. While pulmonary embolism (Option D) also causes respiratory distress and elevated D-dimer, it is less likely to cause early altered mental status or the classic petechial rash often seen in fat embolism. The suggestive X-ray likely shows bilateral patchy infiltrates mimicking ARDS, which is characteristic of this syndrome. Thus, fat embolism is the most consistent post-traumatic diagnosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a fracture visible on X-ray. In this type of fracture, which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a spiral fracture of the humerus midshaft. This fracture type is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve because the nerve courses directly against the bone within the spiral (radial) groove. Trauma at this specific location frequently causes radial nerve palsy, which manifests clinically as "wrist drop"—the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. The median nerve (Option A) is situated medially and is rarely affected by midshaft humeral injuries. The ulnar nerve (Option C) runs near the medial epicondyle and is more commonly injured in distal fractures. The axillary nerve (Option D) is located near the surgical neck of the humerus and is typically injured in proximal fractures or shoulder dislocations. Given the close anatomical proximity of the radial nerve to the humeral shaft, it is the most likely structure to be damaged

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which ligament is tested in the following test?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the Anterior Drawer Test, a common clinical maneuver used to evaluate the integrity of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL). To perform the test, the knee is flexed to 90 degrees, and the examiner pulls the tibia forward while stabilizing the femur. Excessive forward displacement of the tibia indicates an ACL tear. The Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) (Option B) is assessed using the Posterior Drawer Test, where the tibia is pushed backward instead. The Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) (Option C) is tested using the valgus stress test to check for gapping on the inner side of the knee. The Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL) (Option D) is evaluated with the varus stress test to check the outer side of the joint. Because the image shows the tibia being pulled anteriorly, the ACL is the correct target of this specific test

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is brought for a routine health check-up. Which developmental milestone is most commonly expected to be achieved at this age?
options: Creeps well on hands and knees
questions.explanation: By 9 months of age, most infants have achieved the gross motor milestone of creeping well on their hands and knees. They are also beginning to pull themselves up to stand and typically demonstrate an immature pincer grasp. A mature grasp (Option A), specifically the ability to pick up small objects with precision, is typically achieved closer to 12 months. Hopping on one foot (Option C) is a complex gross motor skill that does not develop until approximately 4 years of age. Running steadily (Option D) is a milestone reached around 18 to 24 months as the child gains better coordination. Therefore, at the 9-month check-up, creeping is the most developmentally appropriate skill to expect. Other typical findings at this age include "waving bye-bye" and expressing stranger anxiety

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient develops shortness of breath specifically during physical exertion in cold weather, which is relieved after using salbutamol. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
options: Vagal stimulation due to cold air exposure
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction triggered by cold air
Airway hyperreactivity due to cold-induced asthma exacerbation
questions.explanation: Transient airway narrowing during or after physical activity is known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). In winter, cold and dry air causes heat and moisture loss from the airways, triggering hyperreactivity and subsequent bronchospasm. This condition is classically relieved by short-acting beta-agonists like salbutamol. Vagal stimulation (Option A) usually causes bradycardia or nasal symptoms rather than exercise-specific breathlessness. Decreased cardiac output (Option B) is not the mechanism for respiratory symptoms that respond to bronchodilators. Cold-induced asthma exacerbation (Option D) is a general term, but EIB is the more precise diagnosis when exercise is the specific trigger described. Spirometry or an exercise challenge test is used for diagnosis, while pre-exercise salbutamol inhalation is the standard management to prevent attacks during intense activity in cold environments

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An alcoholic patient is admitted to the hospital 48 hours after his last alcohol intake. He presents with altered consciousness, disorientation, and marked agitation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Delirium tremens (DT) is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically peaking 48–72 hours after the last drink. It is characterized by severe agitation, disorientation, altered consciousness, and autonomic instability (hypertension, tachycardia). This is a medical emergency with a significant mortality rate if untreated. Simple alcohol withdrawal symptoms (Option B) include milder tremors and anxiety that typically appear 6–12 hours after cessation. Cocaine intoxication (Option C) causes agitation but usually occurs immediately after use and presents with dilated pupils (mydriasis). Korsakoff psychosis (Option D) is a chronic thiamine deficiency complication involving permanent memory loss and confabulation rather than acute disorientation and severe agitation. Given the 48-hour timeline and the severity of the mental status changes, DT is the definitive diagnosis requiring ICU monitoring and benzodiazepine therapy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue, anemia, and hepatomegaly, and hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrates the presence of HbS. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS) on electrophoresis confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. Under low oxygen conditions, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis. Hydroxyurea is the primary chronic therapy because it increases the production of fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Higher levels of HbF inhibit the polymerization of HbS, thereby reducing the frequency of painful crises and systemic complications. Blood transfusions (Option B) are reserved for acute severe anemia or emergencies rather than first-line long-term management. Iron supplementation (Option C) is contraindicated unless a concurrent iron deficiency is proven, as these patients are at risk for iron overload from hemolysis and transfusions. Vitamin B12 (Option D) treats macrocytic anemia and is not specific to sickle cell disease. Therefore, hydroxyurea remains the definitive treatment to modify the disease course

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young boy presents with joint swelling after a fall. Lab investigations show normal PT and raised aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Joint swelling (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is a classic indicator of a coagulation factor deficiency, most notably hemophilia. Laboratory findings of a normal PT combined with a prolonged aPTT confirm a defect in the intrinsic pathway. Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) and Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) both manifest with this specific pattern. Von Willebrand Disease (Option A) also shows a raised aPTT but is typically characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding (like epistaxis) rather than deep joint bleeds. Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option C) causes fatigue and pallor but has no effect on coagulation times. Platelet function disorders (Option D) lead to mucosal bleeding and petechiae, while both PT and aPTT usually remain within normal limits. Thus, the isolated aPTT elevation and hemarthrosis identify hemophilia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, dysarthria, and behavioral changes. Examination reveals hepatomegaly and a golden-brown Kayser–Fleischer ring at the corneal limbus, raising suspicion of Wilson’s disease. Which investigation is best to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wilson's Disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and systemic copper accumulation. While low serum ceruloplasmin (Option A) and high urinary copper (Option D) are important screening tools, the gold standard for definitive diagnosis is a liver biopsy with quantitative copper estimation. This directly measures the pathological buildup of the metal in the tissue. Serum copper (Option C) is generally low in these patients because most copper in the blood is normally bound to ceruloplasmin, which is deficient. The presence of a Kayser-Fleischer ring (Option B) is highly suggestive of neurological involvement, but the tissue biopsy remains the most accurate confirmatory test. Management involves long-term chelation therapy or zinc supplements to inhibit further copper absorption

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which CD markers are typically positive in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)?
questions.explanation: The hallmark immunophenotype of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL) involves the expression of mature B-cell markers alongside a specific aberrant T-cell marker. CLL cells typically express CD19, CD20, and CD23. The most distinctive diagnostic feature is the aberrant co-expression of CD5, which is normally found on T-cells. This unique "B-cell plus CD5" profile helps clinicians distinguish CLL from other mature B-cell malignancies. Option A is incorrect as it contains pure T-cell markers like CD3 and CD8. Option B (CD10, CD19, CD22) is characteristic of precursor B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL), where CD10 represents the common ALL antigen (CALLA). Option D consists of myeloid lineage markers such as CD13, CD33, and CD117, which are used to diagnose Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) rather than lymphoid neoplasms. Thus, the presence of CD19, CD20, CD23, and CD5 is definitive for CLL

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with severe anemia, and laboratory evaluation shows a normocytic, normochromic anemia. What is the most appropriate treatment to manage this condition?
questions.explanation: Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is primarily caused by a deficiency in erythropoietin, as the damaged kidneys can no longer produce sufficient amounts of this hormone to stimulate red blood cell production. The resulting anemia is typically normocytic and normochromic. The standard treatment is the administration of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs), such as darbepoetin alfa or epoetin alfa. Folic acid (Option A) and Vitamin B12 (Option B) are used for megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemias and would not correct the underlying hormonal deficit in CKD. Iron chelation therapy (Option D) is used for iron overload, not for treating anemia. While ensuring adequate iron stores is an important supportive step, the core therapeutic intervention for correcting the hormonal lack and associated normocytic anemia in CKD patients is the use of ESAs like darbepoetin alfa

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the eye manifestation seen in HLA B27- positive patients with ulcerative colitis?
questions.explanation: Patients with HLA-B27-positive inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, have a significantly increased risk for extraintestinal autoimmune manifestations. The most classic ocular complication is acute anterior uveitis. It typically presents with sudden eye pain, redness (ciliary flush), photophobia, and blurred vision. Conjunctivitis (Option B) is more common in reactive arthritis and involves a more superficial inflammation. Scleritis (Option C) presents with deep, boring pain and is more often linked to systemic diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. While iridocyclitis (Option D) is a subset of anterior uveitis, the general and clinically preferred term for this broad extraintestinal manifestation in IBD is uveitis. Therefore, uveitis is the standard diagnostic answer for this autoimmune link

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young woman presents with ptosis that shows diurnal variation. CT scan of the chest reveals an anterior mediastinal mass consistent with a thymic tumor. Which receptor is most likely affected in this condition?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ
questions.explanation: The combination of diurnal ptosis (weakness that worsens during the day and improves with rest) and a thymic mass is highly characteristic of Myasthenia Gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies target and destroy the nicotinic acetylcholine (ACh) receptors on the post-synaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). The thymus gland plays a critical role in the pathogenesis, with roughly 15% of MG patients having a thymoma. Presynaptic ACh receptors (Option A) are not the target in MG. Voltage-gated calcium channels (Option C) are targeted in Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome, which is often associated with small cell lung cancer rather than thymoma. Acetylcholinesterase (Option D) is the enzyme that breaks down ACh; while it is inhibited by drugs used to treat MG, it is not the target of the disease's autoantibodies. Thus, the post-synaptic ACh receptor is the site of the defect

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a severe headache. CT imaging of the brain shows hypodense areas in the right basal region, labeled as “X.” What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache is the classic presentation of a Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH). On a non-contrast CT, acute blood appears hyperdense (bright) and typically fills the subarachnoid spaces, including the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures. When blood fills the basal cisterns, it creates the pathognomonic “Star of Death” sign. Hypodense areas may appear later if ischemia develops. Meningococcal meningitis (Option B) usually shows meningeal enhancement but not acute hyperdense cisterns. A brain abscess (Option C) appears as a ring-enhancing lesion with edema. Pneumocephalus (Option D) would show very dark areas representing air rather than bright blood. Therefore, the hyperdense filling of the basal regions on CT, combined with the history of severe headache, confirms the diagnosis of SAH

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a known history of rheumatic heart disease is found on imaging to have an aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: A coronary artery aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm (10–20 mm) is classified as a large aneurysm. Such lesions carry a high risk of complications, including intraluminal thrombosis and distal embolization, which can lead to myocardial infarction. The standard of care for long-term thrombotic risk reduction in these patients is lifelong low-dose aspirin therapy. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with Clopidogrel (Option B) is typically reserved for acute coronary syndromes or giant aneurysms rather than stable large ones. A 3-week course of aspirin (Option C) is insufficient because the risk of clot formation persists as long as the aneurysm is present. IV antibiotics (Option D) are only indicated if there is evidence of an infected (mycotic) aneurysm or active endocarditis. Thus, permanent antiplatelet protection is the cornerstone of management

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A mutation in the SODI gene is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The SOD1 gene encodes superoxide dismutase 1, an enzyme that protects cells from oxidative damage. Mutations in this gene are responsible for approximately 20% of familial Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) cases. The mutant protein misfolds and gains toxic properties, leading to the degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons. Huntington's disease (Option A) is caused by a repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Multiple sclerosis (Option B) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease. Parkinson's disease (Option D) is typically linked to SNCA or LRRK2 genes. ALS is characterized by progressive muscle weakness and spasticity, but sensation and cognition are usually preserved. Thus, SOD1 is a specific genetic marker for the motor neuron degeneration seen in ALS

questions.text: Identify the types of sutures?
options: Simple Interrupted suture (D) Simple Interrupted suture The image displays simple interrupted sutures, which is the most basic and commonly used suturing technique. Each stitch is placed independently, ensuring that if one suture fails or is removed (e.g., for drainage), the remaining stitches continue to hold the wound edges together. Vertical and Horizontal Mattress sutures (Options A and B) are used specifically for wound edge eversion and tension distribution and have a distinct double-pass appearance. Subcuticular sutures (Option C) are placed just beneath the epidermis for an aesthetic finish and are typically not visible on the skin surface as separate loops. The separate, individual loops shown in the image are the hallmark of the simple interrupted technique.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient in the ICU undergoes an attempted subclavian vein catheterization, which is unsuccessful. Soon afterward, the patient develops hypotension with a rising pulse rate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The procedure for subclavian vein catheterization carries a significant risk of accidental pleural injury, which can lead to a pneumothorax. The entry of air into the pleural space reduces venous return to the heart, resulting in sudden hypotension (BP drop) and a reflex tachycardia (pulse rise). In the intensive care unit, this can progress rapidly to a life-threatening tension pneumothorax. Typical clinical signs include unilateral decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on percussion. While displacement or dislodgement of the endotracheal tube (Options B and D) would cause respiratory distress and hypoxia, they are not standard complications of a central line attempt. Air embolism (Option C) is a possible but less common complication that presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and a "mill wheel" murmur. Given the specific context of a failed subclavian attempt followed by hemodynamic instability, pneumothorax is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustains a road traffic accident and has a normal non-contrast CT scan of the head at admission. After several days in the ICU, the patient deteriorates into coma and subsequently dies. Brain biopsy reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a severe primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma, such as a road traffic accident. These forces disrupt axons throughout the white matter, brainstem, and corpus callosum. A classic feature of DAI is that initial Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) scans are often normal or show only minute, subtle abnormalities. Diagnosis is frequently clinical, based on a prolonged coma without a lucid interval, or confirmed via MRI. Histopathology reveals multiple punctate, petechial hemorrhages within deep white matter tracts. Ischemic injury (Option A) typically presents with localized territorial infarcts. Intraventricular bleeding (Option C) and subdural hemorrhage (Option D) would be clearly visible on the initial CT as hyperdense blood collections within the ventricles or as a crescent-shaped mass, respectively. Thus, the normal CT followed by punctate hemorrhages on biopsy is pathognomonic for DAI

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the best confirmatory method to ensure the central line is in the jugular vein?
questions.explanation: Following the insertion of a central venous line, such as in the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray is the gold standard confirmatory method. It serves two vital purposes: verifying the correct anatomical position of the catheter tip (ideally at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium) and ruling out immediate iatrogenic complications like a pneumothorax. While blood color (Option C) and blood pH (Option B) can provide clues about whether a vessel is arterial or venous, they are subjective and unreliable for definitive confirmation. ETCO2 (Option D) is used to confirm endotracheal tube placement, not central line position. Furthermore, if an insertion attempt fails on one side, an X-ray or ultrasound should be performed before attempting the opposite side to prevent bilateral complications. Thus, radiological verification remains the best confirmatory step

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has cheilosis with koilonychia and anemia. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by a classic clinical triad: iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, and glossitis or cheilosis. Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) and cheilosis (cracking at the mouth corners) are physical signs resulting from severe, chronic iron deficiency. This condition is most common in middle-aged women and carries an increased risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated. Esophageal cancer (Option B) may be a long-term complication but is not the primary diagnosis for this triad. Achalasia cardia (Option C) is a motility disorder that causes dysphagia but is not associated with anemia or iron-deficiency skin signs. Tylosis palmaris (Option D) is a genetic condition involving thickened skin on the palms and soles, which is also linked to esophageal cancer risk but unrelated to anemia. Therefore, the described findings are diagnostic of Plummer-Vinson syndrome

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification is used for Barrett esophagus?
questions.explanation: The Prague C & M criteria is the internationally recognized endoscopic classification system used to standardize the reporting of Barrett's esophagus. In this system, "C" represents the circumferential extent of the metaplastic mucosa, and "M" represents the maximal extent (including "tongues" of mucosa) from the gastroesophageal junction. This allows for accurate monitoring and surveillance of the disease. Savary-Miller classification (Option B) is used to grade the severity of reflux esophagitis based on erosions. Johnson classification (Option C) categorizes types of gastric ulcers. Forrest classification (Option D) is used in the setting of acute upper GI bleeding to categorize peptic ulcers based on their bleeding stigmata and to predict the risk of rebleeding. Therefore, for the specific anatomical measurement of Barrett's mucosa, the Prague classification is the only correct choice

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with hematemesis and is found to have splenomegaly on examination. His history reveals that he underwent exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hematemesis (from esophageal varices) and splenomegaly in a young child, particularly with a history of neonatal umbilical vein manipulation (such as exchange transfusion or catheterization), is strongly suggestive of portal vein thrombosis. This is a common cause of pre-hepatic portal hypertension in children. Splenic vein thrombosis (Option A) can cause localized portal hypertension but is less common and doesn't explain the generalized portosystemic shunt as well as the history does. Budd-Chiari syndrome (Option C) involves hepatic vein obstruction and typically presents with hepatomegaly and ascites, which are not the primary features here. Liver cirrhosis (Option D) can cause portal hypertension but is rare in a 5-year-old without a known history of chronic liver disease or metabolic disorders. Thus, the neonatal history is the key to identifying portal vein thrombosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A skin graft was performed on an immuno compromised patient using tissue obtained from another immuno compromised donor. Several weeks later, the recipient developed contractures along with systemic symptoms. What is the most likely underlying cause of this complication?
options: Rejection due to recipient T8 cells
questions.explanation: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and mount an immune attack. This typically occurs when an immunocompromised host is unable to reject the donor cells. In the context of a graft from another immunocompromised individual, donor lymphocytes may still be present. GVHD presents with systemic features such as fever, rash, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction, along with local changes like contractures. Graft failure (Option B) is a local event resulting from poor blood supply leading to early necrosis, not systemic symptoms weeks later. Host-versus-graft rejection (Option C) requires a functioning recipient immune system, which is absent here. Delayed wound healing (Option D) is common in immunocompromised states but does not account for the systemic multi-organ involvement. Therefore, GVHD is the most probable cause

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman presents with a breast lump accompanied by skin dimpling and retraction of the nipple. Involvement of which anatomical structure is most likely responsible for the skin dimpling observed in this case?
questions.explanation: Skin dimpling in cases of breast carcinoma is caused by the malignant infiltration and subsequent contraction of the suspensory ligaments of Cooper. These fibrous bands extend from the deep pectoral fascia through the breast tissue to the dermis. When a tumor invades these ligaments, they shorten and pull the overlying skin inward, creating a "dimpled" or "puckered" appearance. Lactiferous ducts (Option A) are primarily responsible for nipple retraction when they are infiltrated and shortened by a central tumor. Infiltration of the pectoral fascia (Option C) results in fixation of the breast to the chest wall, rather than skin dimpling. Malignant invasion of subcutaneous fat (Option D) contributes to the palpable mass but does not create the dimpling effect. Thus, the mechanical pulling on Cooper's ligaments is the direct anatomical cause of this specific clinical finding

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant has a scrotal swelling present since birth, which has now become acutely painful, erythematous, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The infant has a congenital scrotal mass (likely an inguinal hernia) that has suddenly become painful, erythematous, and irreducible, indicating that the blood supply to the trapped tissue is compromised. This is the definition of a strangulated hernia, a surgical emergency where delayed treatment leads to bowel necrosis. Acute epididymo-orchitis (Option A) is rare in infants and would not involve an irreducible groin mass. Testicular torsion (Option B) presents with acute pain but would not have been present from birth. An incarcerated hernia (Option D) is irreducible but does not yet have vascular compromise; therefore, it lacks the severe redness and systemic tenderness seen in strangulation. Physical examination shows a tense, extremely tender mass with no cough impulse. Immediate resuscitation followed by surgical exploration is mandatory

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury of the arm. On the sixth postoperative day, he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area
questions.explanation: By post-operative day 6, a split-thickness skin graft is in the early phase of fibrovascular ingrowth. If the patient develops stiffness during movement, the most appropriate management is passive extension under direct visualization. This allows the therapist to gently increase the range of motion while ensuring that the graft is not experiencing shearing forces that could cause displacement or partial loss. Surgical excision of contractures (Option A) is only performed on mature, months-old scars, not on a fresh graft. Continuing physiotherapy blindly (Option C) risks damaging the fragile graft if the stiffness is due to improper adhesion. Removing the graft (Option D) is unnecessary unless there is clear evidence of total graft failure, such as infection or necrosis. Thus, cautious supervised movement is the preferred rehabilitation strategy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a recommended treatment for esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the first-line treatment for both the management of acute variceal hemorrhage and secondary prophylaxis. It involves placing elastic bands around the varices to cause thrombosis and eventual obliteration. TIPS (Option B) is an effective procedure but is reserved as a salvage therapy when endoscopic and pharmacological treatments fail to control bleeding. Intravenous labetalol (Option C) is not used; instead, non-selective beta-blockers like propranolol are used for primary prophylaxis to reduce portal pressure. While prophylactic antibiotics are standard in variceal bleeding (usually ceftriaxone), oral amoxicillin (Option D) is not the standard choice and has no role in the direct control of bleeding. Thus, EVL is the definitive recommended endoscopic intervention

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of ulcer?
questions.explanation: The ulcer shown is located in the gaiter area (the medial aspect of the lower leg), which is the classic site for a venous ulcer. These ulcers result from chronic venous insufficiency and are typically shallow with irregular, sloping edges. Arterial ulcers (Option A) are usually found on the toes or heels, are very painful, and have "punched-out" edges. Diabetic and Neuropathic ulcers (Options C and D) typically occur on the weight-bearing pressure points of the foot, such as the metatarsal heads or the heel, and are often painless due to associated neuropathy. The location and appearance of the lesion in the image are pathognomonic for venous disease

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Given below what is the correct sequence of Damage control surgery? 1. Patient selection 2. Primary exploration 3. ICU care 4. Secondary exploration
questions.explanation: Damage Control Surgery (DCS) is a specialized surgical strategy for unstable trauma patients. The sequence is: 1. Patient selection: Identifying physiologically "exhausted" patients who cannot tolerate a definitive operation. 2. Primary exploration: An abbreviated surgery to control hemorrhage and contamination. 3. ICU care: Stabilization in the ICU to correct the "lethal triad" of acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy. 4. Secondary exploration: Returning to the OR for definitive repair once the patient is stable. Any other sequence, such as those in Options B, C, or D, would violate the physiological principles of DCS. Therefore, the 1-2-3-4 sequence is the only standard protocol

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst?
options: Resection of the cyst along with the adjacent bowel
questions.explanation: Chylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are benign, well-encapsulated lymphatic malformations. Because they typically do not infiltrate the intestinal wall and have a blood supply independent of the bowel, complete enucleation is the preferred treatment. This allows for total removal of the cyst while preserving the adjacent intestine. Aspiration (Option A) is inadequate due to extremely high rates of recurrence and risk of infection. Resection of the adjacent bowel (Option C) is only necessary if the cyst is firmly adherent to mesenteric vessels or has an enterogenous origin. Conservative management (Option D) is avoided because these cysts can cause complications like torsion, hemorrhage, or rupture. Therefore, surgical enucleation is the definitive standard of care

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During assisted vaginal delivery, where is the vacuum device typically applied?
options: At 3 cm behind the anterior fontanelle
3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
Between the anterior and posterior fontanelle
questions.explanation: In vacuum-assisted delivery, the cup must be placed over the flexion point. This point is located on the sagittal suture, approximately 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle. Placing the cup here ensures that traction results in maximum flexion of the fetal head, allowing the smallest possible diameter (suboccipitobregmatic) to present to the birth canal. Applying the cup behind the anterior fontanelle (Option A) would cause deflexion, increasing the presenting diameter and risk of failure. Placement directly on the posterior fontanelle (Option B) or generalized between the fontanelles (Option D) does not achieve optimal mechanical leverage for head flexion. Therefore, the specific 3 cm anterior position is critical for a safe and successful procedure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is planned for laparoscopic surgery under general anesthesia as a day care procedure. Which of the following factors would make him unsuitable for day care surgery?
options: Home is 45 minutes away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
The patient has had general anesthesia in the past without complications
questions.explanation: The presence of a responsible adult attendant at home for the first 24 hours is a non-negotiable safety requirement for day care (ambulatory) surgery under general anesthesia.
